title: 48. Numeracy & Number Systems: Rational Numbers on a Number Line
description: A comprehensive mathematics curriculum progressing from foundational numeracy and core mathematical concepts to algebra, geometry, calculus, linear algebra, probability, statistics, discrete mathematics, optimization, mathematical foundations of AI, advanced pure mathematics, and emerging research methods.

questions.concept: Locating Negative Fractions on a Number Line
questions.learningObjective: Locate a negative fraction between consecutive integers on a number line.
questions.question: On a number line, where is \(-\frac{3}{4}\) located?

options.label: A
options.text: Between \(-1\) and \(0\), three-fourths of a unit to the left of \(0\).

options.label: B
options.text: Between \(0\) and \(1\), three-fourths of a unit to the right of \(0\).

questions.explanation: The number \(-\frac{3}{4}\) is negative, so it lies to the left of \(0\). Its distance from \(0\) is \(\frac{3}{4}\) unit, which places it between \(-1\) and \(0\). Therefore, it is three-fourths of a unit to the left of \(0\).
questions.hint: First decide which side of \(0\) contains negative numbers, then use the fraction's magnitude to locate the point.

questions.concept: Finding a Coordinate from Equal Intervals
questions.learningObjective: Determine the rational-number coordinate halfway between two marked values on a number line.
questions.question: A point \(P\) is exactly halfway between \(\frac{1}{2}\) and \(\frac{3}{2}\) on a number line. What is the coordinate of \(P\)?
questions.explanation: The distance from \(\frac{1}{2}\) to \(\frac{3}{2}\) is \(1\). Half of this distance is \(\frac{1}{2}\). Starting at \(\frac{1}{2}\) and moving \(\frac{1}{2}\) unit to the right gives \(1\). Therefore, \(P\) is at \(1\).
questions.hint: Find the distance between the two coordinates, then move half of that distance from the smaller coordinate toward the larger one.

questions.concept: Ordering Rational Numbers on a Number Line
questions.learningObjective: Order fractions and decimals from left to right on a number line.
questions.question: Which list gives the numbers \(-1.25\), \(-\frac{3}{4}\), and \(\frac{1}{2}\) in their correct order from left to right on a number line?
questions.explanation: On a number line, smaller numbers lie farther left. Since \(-1.25<-\frac{3}{4}<\frac{1}{2}\), the correct left-to-right order is \(-1.25\), \(-\frac{3}{4}\), \(\frac{1}{2}\).
questions.hint: Convert the fraction to a decimal if helpful, then compare the values from least to greatest.

questions.learningObjective: Recognize equivalent fraction and decimal representations of the same point on a number line.
questions.question: A point on a number line has coordinate \(0.6\). Which fraction labels the same point?
questions.explanation: The decimal \(0.6\) equals \(\frac{6}{10}\), which simplifies to \(\frac{3}{5}\). Equivalent rational numbers occupy the same point on a number line. Therefore, \(\frac{3}{5}\) labels the same point.
questions.hint: Write the decimal as a fraction with denominator \(10\), then simplify.

questions.learningObjective: Calculate the distance between two rational-number coordinates on a number line.
questions.question: Points \(A\) and \(B\) are located at \(-\frac{2}{3}\) and \(\frac{1}{3}\), respectively. What is the distance between them on the number line?
questions.explanation: Distance on a number line is the absolute difference of the coordinates: \(\left|\frac{1}{3}-\left(-\frac{2}{3}\right)\right|=\left|\frac{3}{3}\right|=1\). Therefore, the points are \(1\) unit apart.
questions.hint: Subtract one coordinate from the other and take the absolute value.

questions.learningObjective: Compare negative rational numbers by their positions on a number line.
questions.question: Point \(M\) is at \(-\frac{5}{4}\), and point \(N\) is at \(-1.1\). Which point is farther to the right on the number line?
questions.explanation: Convert \(-\frac{5}{4}\) to decimal form: \(-\frac{5}{4}=-1.25\). Since \(-1.1>-1.25\), \(-1.1\) lies farther to the right. Therefore, point \(N\) is farther to the right.
questions.hint: For negative numbers, the value closer to \(0\) is farther to the right.

questions.learningObjective: Determine the midpoint between two rational-number coordinates on a number line.
questions.question: Point \(C\) is at \(-\frac{1}{2}\) and point \(D\) is at \(\frac{3}{2}\). What is the coordinate of the point exactly halfway between \(C\) and \(D\)?
questions.explanation: The midpoint is the average of the two coordinates: \(\frac{-\frac{1}{2}+\frac{3}{2}}{2}=\frac{1}{2}\). Equivalently, the two points are \(2\) units apart, so moving \(1\) unit right from \(-\frac{1}{2}\) reaches \(\frac{1}{2}\).
questions.hint: Find the distance between the two points and move half that distance from either endpoint toward the other.

questions.concept: Movement on a Rational Number Line
questions.learningObjective: Determine a final rational-number coordinate after a directed movement on a number line.
questions.question: A point starts at \(\frac{1}{3}\) on a number line and moves \(\frac{7}{6}\) units to the left. At which coordinate does it stop?
questions.explanation: Moving left means subtracting the distance. Convert \(\frac{1}{3}\) to sixths: \(\frac{1}{3}=\frac{2}{6}\). Then \(\frac{2}{6}-\frac{7}{6}=-\frac{5}{6}\). Therefore, the point stops at \(-\frac{5}{6}\).
questions.hint: Represent a move to the left by subtraction, and use a common denominator before calculating.

questions.concept: Analyzing Relative Positions of Rational Numbers
questions.learningObjective: Analyze the relative positions of fraction and decimal coordinates and a midpoint on a number line.
questions.question: Point \(R\) is at \(-0.4\), and point \(S\) is at \(-\frac{3}{8}\). Point \(T\) is exactly halfway between \(R\) and \(S\). Which statement is correct?

options.label: A
options.text: Point \(T\) is to the right of \(R\) and to the left of \(S\).

options.label: B
options.text: Point \(T\) is to the left of \(R\) and to the right of \(S\).

questions.explanation: Convert \(-\frac{3}{8}\) to decimal form: \(-\frac{3}{8}=-0.375\). Thus \(-0.4<-0.375\), so \(R\) is to the left of \(S\). A midpoint between two distinct points lies between them. In fact, its coordinate is \(\frac{-0.4+(-0.375)}{2}=-0.3875\), and \(-0.4<-0.3875<-0.375\). Therefore, \(T\) is to the right of \(R\) and to the left of \(S\).
questions.hint: Convert both coordinates to decimals to decide which of \(R\) and \(S\) is farther left; the midpoint lies between them.

questions.concept: Reasoning About Distance in a Rational Interval
questions.learningObjective: Identify a rational-number coordinate within an interval by comparing its distances from the endpoints.
questions.question: Which rational number lies strictly between \(-\frac{2}{5}\) and \(\frac{1}{10}\) and is closer to \(\frac{1}{10}\) than to \(-\frac{2}{5}\)?
questions.explanation: The endpoints are \(-\frac{2}{5}=-0.4\) and \(\frac{1}{10}=0.1\). Both options lie between them. For \(-\frac{1}{4}=-0.25\), the distances to the endpoints are \(0.15\) and \(0.35\), so it is closer to \(-0.4\). For \(-\frac{1}{10}=-0.1\), the distances are \(0.3\) from \(-0.4\) and \(0.2\) from \(0.1\). Therefore, \(-\frac{1}{10}\) satisfies both conditions.
questions.hint: Check both conditions separately: first whether each option lies inside the interval, then compare its distance from each endpoint.
